name: Ignoratio elenchi
statement: Ignoratio elenchi is proving something other than the point at issue, so an argument can be sound and still leave the question it was raised to settle open.
meaning: The Latin tag means ignorance of refutation, and it names the odd item on Aristotle's list. His other twelve fallacies are bad deductions that look like good ones. This one can be a good deduction that ends in the wrong place, which is how Hans Hansen describes it in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: the exception in which the deduction contains no fallacy but the conclusion proved only appears to contradict the answerer's thesis. Aristotle defines refutation tightly. It contradicts one and the same attribute, not the name but the reality, from the propositions granted, without counting in the original point, and 'in the same respect and relation and manner and time in which it was asserted'. Miss any one condition and something has been proved, but not the thing denied. His examples are dull on purpose. Two is double of one and not double of three, so a man who shows that the same thing is both double and not double has refuted nobody. Richard Whately fixed the English sense in the nineteenth century, calling it irrelevant conclusion and filing the ad-arguments beneath it. The term has carried both jobs since, a named error and a heading for anything off the point.

origin.where: Elements of Logic, fourth edition, printed for B. Fellowes, London
origin.note: The fallacy is Aristotle's, from On Sophistical Refutations, and the year here is Whately's. Whately puts it among the material or non-logical fallacies, the case 'when the Conclusion is not the one required, but irrelevant', because the argument offered 'is not the elenchus (i. e. proof of the contradictory) of your opponent's assertion, which it should be; but proves, instead of that, some other proposition resembling it'. He would drop the Latin name if he could, and keeps it because it is 'so generally adopted as absolutely to require some mention to be made of it'. The copy read here is the fourth edition, revised, whose title page names B. Fellowes of Ludgate Street and describes the book as comprising the substance of the article in the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana. The Library of Congress scan is catalogued as 1831. No earlier edition was obtained and no first-publication date is claimed.

evidence: No experiment was located, so the evidence is a set of documents. Aristotle sorts apparent refutations into six that depend on language and seven that do not, and the third of the seven is 'that which depends upon ignorance of what refutation is'. That makes it the thirteenth of thirteen and one member of the list. Chapter 6 then opens differently, and this is the passage the textbooks compress. 'The right way, then, is either to divide apparent proofs and refutations as above, or else to refer them all to ignorance of what refutation is, and make that our starting-point: for it is possible to analyse all the aforesaid modes of fallacy into breaches of the definition of a refutation.' Two things follow from the wording. The reduction is offered as an alternative to the division, one of two ways of arranging the same material, and its scope is the modes of fallacy already set out rather than fallacies at large. Aristotle then walks the list. Accident fails because a proof about an accident of a thing is not a proof about the thing. Secundum quid fails because the affirmation and the denial are not about the same point. Begging the question fails the clause that bars counting in the original point, non-cause fails the clause requiring the conclusion to follow from the premisses, and many questions fails because a proposition is a single statement about a single thing. Hansen reports the same split in the modern literature. On one reading ignoratio elenchi is the thirteenth fallacy, on another it is not a separate fallacy but an alternative to the language-dependent classification of the other twelve. Whately's chapter is where the catch-all habit starts. He lists the argumentum ad hominem, ad verecundiam and ad populum as arguments 'which we should by no means universally call Fallacies; but which when unfairly used, and so far as they are fallacious, may very well be referred to the present head'. He also gives the move a second face, proving part of what was required and dwelling on it, and his example is a university charged with teaching only elementary mathematics whose defender argues that some of its books are elementary. Bradley Dowden's list of 231 fallacies in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy keeps the wide sense: irrelevant conclusion is where ignoratio elenchi and missing the point both point, and ad hominem, appeal to authority, appeal to emotions and argument from ignorance are given as other examples of it. Douglas Walton argues the wide sense has cost the term its edge, and that 'historically the ignoratio elenchi has tended to become a rag-bag category to cover any argument where the author is uncertain why it is fallacious'. He credits Charles Hamblin with the underlying objection, that calling a failure of relevance a fallacy is no help until relevance has been defined. Walton tests the cleanest candidate definition, shared subject matter, and it fails in both directions. Two arguments William of Sherwood classed as ignorance of refutation overlap in subject matter and are still bad, and the standard textbook case of a senator answering a charge that Windsor is grimy by praising its schools and its tolerant people overlaps at every premiss. Pragma-dialectics gives the move a rule of its own. Frans van Eemeren and Rob Grootendorst set out ten rules for a critical discussion and place this fallacy under the fourth: rule 4 is violated at the argumentation stage 'by putting forward argumentation that does not refer to the standpoint under discussion as advanced at the confrontation stage (irrelevant argumentation or ignoratio elenchi)'.

replication.headline: No experiment testing whether an irrelevant conclusion persuades anyone, or whether readers notice one, was found. The pragma-dialectical programme that puts rule-breaking moves to ordinary readers has published on four of the ten rules, and the relevance rule is not among them.
replication.detail: The place such a study would sit is the Amsterdam work on judgements of reasonableness, which shows untrained readers discussion fragments containing fallacious and non-fallacious moves and asks them to rate how reasonable each is. Its book-length report is van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels in 2009. Its nine chapters were resolved one by one at Crossref and run continuously to page 224. Two chapters set out the design, one is an exemplary study of ad hominem, four cover the freedom rule, the obligation to defend across two chapters and the argument scheme rule, one covers the concluding rule, and the last draws the programme together. None covers rule 4. That is a statement about the chapter list deposited at Crossref, not about everything those authors have run, and the book itself was not obtained. The nearest experiment located is a fallacy-recognition study rather than a study of this fallacy. Annika Svedholm-Häkkinen and Mika Kiikeri gave participants 63 fallacious and 57 reasonable arguments to rate under instructions to think intuitively or analytically, and recorded responses, response times and cursor trajectories. Their fallacy types are ad hominem, straw man, reference to irrelevant authorities, ad ignorantiam, ad baculum, ad consequentiam, false dilemma, circular argument, slippery slope, non sequitur, statistical fallacies, mixing correlation with causation, post hoc ergo propter hoc and unfalsifiability. The irrelevant conclusion is not among the fourteen. Their result is about how the ratings were reached rather than about any one fallacy: instructions to think analytically made people spend longer without making them change their minds more often.

limits: The search for an experiment covered Europe PMC, Crossref and general web search. Europe PMC returns 29 records for the phrase 'ignoratio elenchi', and the ones inspected are clinical and polemical uses of the term in commentary, correspondence and replies, mostly in medicine. A search there for 'irrelevant conclusion' with fallacy and participants returns two records, one on pre-service teachers analysing claims about covid-19 and one a commentary on norms in the psychology of reasoning, and neither tests the fallacy. Crossref searches on the term return the Walton paper, the Oxford English Dictionary entry and a run of journal correspondence using the phrase as an accusation. What could not be settled is where the boundary sits between this entry and the red herring. Walton's paper treats the two as one thing, and Dowden's encyclopedia files the irrelevant conclusion as a form of the red herring, while Hansen's article names the straw man as a variation of ignoratio elenchi. Aristotle's cases are not diversions at all. Nothing was found that adjudicates between these arrangements, and the entry describes them rather than choosing. On the texts, Aristotle was read only in the Pickard-Cambridge English translation, in two separate transcriptions that agree on every phrase quoted here. Both carry one paragraph twice, on begging the question and non-cause, which is why nothing is claimed about how many times Aristotle makes that point. No Greek text and no second translator were obtained, so the Bekker numbers usually attached to these passages are not printed here. William of Sherwood's examples are quoted through Walton, who takes them from Kretzmann's 1966 translation at page 156, and neither the translation nor the Latin was obtained. Hamblin's Fallacies of 1970 was not obtained, and the objection attributed to him is Walton's report of it. The pragma-dialectical rule 4 wording comes from a web reprint of van Eemeren and Grootendorst's chapter in Hansen and Pinto's Fallacies: Classical and Contemporary Readings of 1995, not from the book. Whately was read in an optical transcription of a library scan, which garbles the date on the title page, so the year comes from the archive's catalogue record for that scan. The Oxford English Dictionary entry for the term was located at Crossref and is paywalled, so nothing about the term's first attestation in English is stated here.
misreadings: The commonest error is that Aristotle called this the master fallacy, to which every other one reduces. What chapter 6 offers is a choice between two ways of dividing the same thirteen: sort them by whether they depend on language, or refer them all to the definition of refutation. The second is a classification, not a ranking, and its reach is the modes he has just enumerated. Hansen sets out both readings and endorses neither. The second error is to treat the wide and narrow senses as the same claim. In the narrow sense the argument is valid, its premisses may be true, and it proves a proposition adjacent to the one denied. In the wide sense the label covers appeals to pity, to force and to the crowd, which fail for reasons of their own, and Walton's objection is that calling all of them failures of relevance explains nothing until relevance is defined. Whately, who did more than anyone to widen the term, was careful where later textbooks are not: he calls the ad-arguments fallacious only when unfairly used. A third error is to hear the charge as settled once made. Naming a conclusion irrelevant is a claim about what the dispute was for, and that is what disputants disagree about. Walton's test case is a senator who answers the charge that his city is grimy by praising its flower parks, its schools and its tolerant citizens. Every premiss is about the city, so shared subject matter cannot be the criterion, and the argument still fails, because tolerant citizens do not make a city clean. The last error is to assume the tactic works. Nothing found here measures whether an audience notices an irrelevant conclusion or is moved by one, and an absence of measurement is not a finding either way.

sources.text: Aristotle. On Sophistical Refutations, translated by W. A. Pickard-Cambridge. Read in full as the Internet Classics Archive plain-text edition. Source for the list of six language-dependent and seven language-independent fallacies, for the definition of refutation, and for the chapter 6 passage quoted here.

Aristotle. On Sophistical Refutations, translated by W. A. Pickard-Cambridge. A second transcription of the same translation, read as a 32-page PDF. Used to confirm every phrase quoted from the first. Both transcriptions carry the paragraph on begging the question and non-cause twice.

Whately, R. Elements of Logic, comprising the substance of the article in the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana, fourth edition revised. London: B. Fellowes. Read in the Internet Archive's optical transcription of the Library of Congress scan, catalogued 1831. Source for the definition of the fallacy, for the treatment of the ad-arguments, and for the fallacy of proving a part instead of the whole.

Hansen, H. (2024). Fallacies. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Read as the entry's own HTML rather than through a summary. Source for the two readings of ignoratio elenchi in Aristotle, for the description of it as the exception among his fallacies, and for the accounts of Whately, Copi and Mill referred to here.

Dowden, B. Fallacies. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Read as the page's own HTML. Source for the wide modern usage, in which irrelevant conclusion absorbs ignoratio elenchi and missing the point, and ad hominem, appeal to authority, appeal to emotions and argument from ignorance are given as examples of it.

Walton, D. N. (1984). Ignoratio Elenchi: The Red Herring Fallacy. Informal Logic, 2(3). Five-page article read in full as the journal's open-access PDF; the scan's optical text is poor and only phrases legible in it are quoted. Source for the rag-bag quotation, for the attribution to Hamblin, for the William of Sherwood examples and for the Windsor case.

van Eemeren, F. H., & Grootendorst, R. (1995). The Pragma-Dialectical Approach to Fallacies. In H. V. Hansen & R. C. Pinto (eds), Fallacies: Classical and Contemporary Readings. Read as a web reprint rather than in the book. Source for the placing of irrelevant argumentation under rule 4 and for the wording quoted here.

van Eemeren, F. H., Garssen, B., & Meuffels, B. (2009). Fallacies and Judgments of Reasonableness. Argumentation Library. Springer. Not obtained. Its nine chapter DOIs were resolved individually at Crossref; the titles and page ranges given here come from those records.

Svedholm-Häkkinen, A. M., & Kiikeri, M. (2022). Cognitive miserliness in argument literacy? Effects of intuitive and analytic thinking on recognizing fallacies. Judgment and Decision Making, 17(2), 331-361. Open access under CC BY. Full text read as the journal's PDF. Source for the stimulus counts, the list of fourteen fallacy types and the result quoted here.
ignoratio elenchi, n. Oxford English Dictionary. Located at Crossref and paywalled; not read. Named here so a reader can find the dictionary record, and nothing on this page rests on it.
